region: Amazon basin floodplains — Peru, Brazil & Bolivia
description: A dwarf cichlid of leaf-litter shallows along the Amazon's floodplain lakes and creeks, the male recognised by his spade-shaped tail edged in red and blue. One male's territory spans several females' caves, and each female guards her own brood alone.

A German-bred line of Agassiz's dwarf cichlid in which the male's dorsal fin and spade-shaped tail are flooded with deep red. Behaviour and care are those of the wild species, including the harem breeding system.
A line-bred strain whose males wear an orange-red wash over body and fins, strongest on the face, belly and tail. It shares the wild species' biology and harem breeding.
A strain selected for the most intense red in the males' unpaired fins, the spade tail almost solid crimson with only a narrow pale base. Females remain yellow with a black band.

Named for the crest of elongated front dorsal spines that the big-mouthed male raises in display. One of the hardiest Apistogramma, it lives in small, often stagnant forest creeks and pools and keeps a harem of females, each spawning in her own cave.
A line-bred cockatoo cichlid whose males carry solid red in both the crested dorsal fin and the lyre-shaped tail. It has the wild species' hardiness and harem breeding.
A line-bred strain in which the dorsal, caudal and anal fins of males are all solid red, the most intensely coloured of the cockatoo cichlid forms. Females stay yellow with black markings.

A popular strain whose males show bright orange bands through the dorsal fin and the upper and lower edges of the lyre tail, with an orange flush on the lower flank. Care and behaviour match the wild species.

region: Paraguay–Paraná basin — Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia & Argentina
description: A small, comparatively peaceful Apistogramma from shallow, plant-filled marshes of the Pantanal and Chaco, tolerating cooler water than most of its genus. Males have a yellow head and spread a tall "umbrella" dorsal fin in display.
A line-bred umbrella cichlid in which the blue sheen of the male spreads over the whole body as an opalescent glow behind a golden head. It keeps the cool-tolerant, peaceful nature of the wild form.

region: Río Meta basin around Villavicencio, Colombia (upper Orinoco)
description: A robust Apistogramma of clear and blackwater llanos streams, the male's tail framed by a broad red seam above a dark submarginal band. Females spawn in caves and lead their fry over the leaf litter.
A dwarf cichlid of shallow savanna creeks; males have red streaks across the cheeks and red-striped dorsal and tail fins over a greenish-blue body. It needs soft, acidic water to breed.

A steep-headed dwarf cichlid from Colombian llanos streams whose males flush red over the throat and lower face. Like its relative A. macmasteri it is a harem-polygynous cave spawner of soft, warm water.

region: Paraguay & Guaporé basins — Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A small, blue-sheened dwarf cichlid of shallow, vegetated marshes, marked by a lateral band plus a second dark stripe angling from the pectoral fin toward the belly. Males raise strongly elongated front dorsal spines when displaying.

Males of this slender species carry some of the longest front dorsal membranes in the genus, raised like a crest in display. Its two parallel dark stripes run along the flank and lower side, over leaf-litter shallows of forest streams.

region: Río Ucayali basin near Jenaro Herrera, Peru
description: Brooding females turn lemon-yellow with three bold black panda blotches on eye, flank and tail base, far more striking than the blue-grey, red-tailed males. A blackwater species that breeds only in very soft, acidic water.

region: Río Ucayali basin near Pucallpa, Peru
description: A close relative of the panda dwarf cichlid: males are pale blue-grey with a smoky tail ringed in red, and brooding females turn yellow with black blotches. It inhabits soft, tannin-stained forest streams.

Long known in the trade as Apistogramma sp. 'Inca 50', this species pairs a yellow body and black lateral band with turquoise streaks across the male's face. It lives in clear, slow forest streams of the Peruvian Andean foothills.

A blackwater dwarf cichlid whose males combine a sail-like dorsal fin with an orange-red throat and cheeks over a greenish body. It needs very soft, acidic water and is shy among roots and leaf litter.

region: Middle Rio Negro around Barcelos, Brazil
description: A blackwater specialist of the Rio Negro whose males show turquoise sheen, elongated dorsal lappets and red lines in the unpaired fins. It is among the most demanding Apistogramma, breeding only in extremely soft, acidic water.

A tiny, slender Apistogramma of Rio Negro blackwater, named for the two parallel dark bands along its flank. It lives among leaf litter in extremely soft, acidic water and is one of the smallest members of the genus.

A comparatively large, slender Apistogramma of clear and whitewater forest streams in the upper Amazon, with a dark lateral band and red-edged unpaired fins in males. Each female spawns in her own cave and guards the brood.

One of the largest Apistogramma, from Guiana Shield rivers; males grow a lyre-shaped tail and greenish iridescence over the head. It is hardier than most of its genus and tolerates near-neutral water.

region: Lower Rio Negro & Amazon near Manaus, Brazil
description: A small, slim Apistogramma of blackwater leaf-litter banks around the Rio Negro mouth; males have elongated front dorsal spines and a dark lateral band over a pale yellowish body. It is shy and best kept with very small, peaceful fishes.

region: Middle Amazon & lower Rio Negro, Brazil
description: A small, yellowish Apistogramma with a dark lateral band ending in a spot at the tail base, found in shallow, leaf-strewn forest streams. Males are only modestly larger and more colourful than females.

region: Upper Paraguay basin & Pantanal — Brazil, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: A small, peaceful Apistogramma of shallow, vegetated Pantanal waters; males show turquoise streaks on the face and a row of dark blotches along the flank. It tolerates cooler, harder water than its Amazonian relatives.

Described in 2008, this was the first Apistogramma found to mouthbrood: after spawning in a cave the female may take eggs and larvae into her mouth. It is a robust, large-headed species with a broad dark band along the flank.

The ram's larger, hardier cousin from the Bolivian and Brazilian lowlands, with black-tipped front dorsal spines and a red-fringed tail with trailing tips. Pairs sift sand together and spawn on a flat stone, both parents guarding the fry.

A line-bred ram in which the blue spangling has spread into a solid electric-blue body, usually with a golden forehead. It needs the same warm, soft water as the wild type but is generally less robust.
A xanthistic line-bred ram with the black pigment largely suppressed, leaving a golden body, orange-red head and faint blue spangles. Its biology and breeding match the wild species.
A line-bred ram with a genetically shortened, compressed spine that gives a rounded, balloon-like body. It keeps the German blue colouring but swims less efficiently than the wild form.

region: Coastal rivers of Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: A metallic green-gold dwarf cichlid of slow, shaded Guianan creeks. In brood dress the female turns yellow with a bold black checkerboard and drives off every intruder, including the much larger male.

Named for the golden head of the male, this Nannacara has a metallic blue-green body with dark-edged scales. As in its relatives, the brooding female turns pale with a dark checkerboard and guards the fry alone.
A rare dwarf acara of the blackwater upper Rio Negro, cream-coloured with bold black bars and a red-fringed dorsal fin. Pairs share brood care and need extremely soft, acidic water.

A peaceful little acara of shallow, vegetated Amazonian backwaters, named for its steeply curved head and wearing a blue-spangled face. Pairs spawn on a cleaned leaf or stone and both parents guard the fry.

region: Paraguay & Guaporé basins — Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A small acara of marshy Pantanal and Chaco waters; in breeding dress the throat and breast flush deep red and a black spot shows in the front of the dorsal fin. Pairs spawn on stones and guard the brood together.

region: Rio Negro & upper Orinoco — Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: A dwarf cichlid of acid blackwater creeks patterned with two rows of dark rectangular blotches; males grow lyre-shaped tails with long trailing filaments. Females spawn on leaves and guard the brood alone.

A checkerboard cichlid of the lower Amazon that lacks the lyre tail of D. filamentosus; males instead show broad, red-edged and spotted unpaired fins. It needs soft, acidic water and peaceful company.

region: Amazon basin (Peru, Ecuador, Colombia & Brazil) & Essequibo, Guyana
description: A protogynous hermaphrodite: fish mature as checkerboard-patterned females, and dominant ones later change sex into larger males covered in a red-and-blue hexagonal mosaic. It lives over sand and leaf litter in soft Amazonian streams.

region: Middle Amazon & lower Rio Negro, Brazil
description: A slender, torpedo-shaped dwarf cichlid of blackwater leaf litter, closely related to Apistogramma. Males have a pointed, lance-shaped tail; females spawn in tiny caves and guard the brood alone.

region: Amazon basin & Essequibo — Peru, Colombia, Brazil & Guyana
description: A small eartheater-like cichlid of slow, sandy Amazonian rivers, with turquoise lines across the cheeks and a dark spot high on the flank below the soft dorsal fin. Groups sift sand for food; breeding pairs spawn on open substrate and guard the brood together.

region: Orinoco & Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: A close relative of the cupid cichlid from the Orinoco and Rio Negro, with a large dark spot on the upper flank and blue lines across the face. It favours soft, acidic water over fine sand and is easily stressed by boisterous tankmates.

region: Lower & middle Amazon, Brazil — incl. Xingu, Tapajós & Tocantins
description: A large eartheater of clear, sandy Amazonian rivers whose every scale carries a turquoise spangle. Groups take mouthful after mouthful of sand and sieve out invertebrates through the gills; pairs spawn on a stone and later carry the larvae in their mouths.

An Orinoco member of the G. surinamensis group with rows of iridescent spangles along the flank and red-streaked, filament-tipped unpaired fins. It sifts sand constantly and the parents carry the larvae in their mouths.

region: Orinoco, Casiquiare & upper Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: An eartheater of the Orinoco and Casiquiare named for the forked dark bar that runs through its large black mid-flank spot. Groups forage over sand, and the parents carry their larvae in their mouths.

region: Coastal rivers of Suriname & French Guiana
description: The true Suriname eartheater of the Guianas' coastal rivers; much stock sold under this name is actually G. proximus or G. altifrons. Males show red-orange lines along the flank and red-tipped dorsal filaments.

A widespread Amazonian eartheater long sold as G. surinamensis, with a black spot mid-flank, iridescent blue lines and orange-tipped dorsal lappets. Pairs spawn on a stone and take the larvae into their mouths.

region: Coastal drainages of eastern & southern Brazil and Uruguay
description: The pearl cichlid of Brazil's Atlantic coastal rivers and lagoons, olive to brown and covered in pearly blue spangles around a black flank spot. Unlike most Geophagus it is an open substrate spawner, and it tolerates cool, hard and even slightly brackish water.

region: Magdalena & Lake Maracaibo basins — Colombia & Venezuela
description: Males of this Andean-foothill eartheater grow a fleshy red nuchal hump in breeding condition. Unlike Amazonian Geophagus, the female alone broods the eggs in her mouth from spawning until the fry swim free.

region: Atrato & San Juan basins, western Colombia
description: A Colombian eartheater whose breeding males grow a golden-yellow nuchal hump above a blue-sheened body with a bold black flank spot. As in G. steindachneri, the female broods the eggs in her mouth.

An undescribed eartheater from the Rio Tapajós whose adults wear an orange-red head above blue-spangled flanks and a black mid-flank spot. It is a delayed mouthbrooder: eggs are laid on a stone and the hatched larvae are carried in the parents' mouths.

region: Paraguay–Paraná basin — Paraguay, Argentina, Brazil & Bolivia
description: Males of this subtropical eartheater develop a towering nuchal hump and an almost vertical forehead. The female takes the larvae into her mouth a few days after spawning, and the species prefers somewhat cooler water than Amazonian Geophagus.

region: Lower Uruguay basin & coastal lagoons — southern Brazil, Uruguay & Argentina
description: A subtropical eartheater named for the rows of iridescent blue stripes along its flanks; it needs a cool winter period to stay healthy. Pairs spawn on open substrate and guard their brood together.

region: Uruguay & lower Paraná basins — southern Brazil, Uruguay & Argentina
description: A small subtropical eartheater whose males show red spots across the dorsal fin and an iridescent blue head. Pairs spawn on open substrate and both guard the fry; it needs cool water in winter.

region: Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil & Uruguay
description: A robust subtropical eartheater whose breeding males develop a nuchal hump and an iridescent, pearly face. The female carries the larvae in her mouth, and the species lives in clear, cool rivers and lagoons.
A long-snouted eartheater of sandy Amazonian rivers, its eyes set high on the head and its cheeks lined in turquoise. Groups sift sand continually, and the pair carries the larvae in their mouths.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco — Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: A blackwater eartheater of the Rio Negro and Orinoco, golden with large black spots on the mid-flank and at the tail base. Sensitive to water quality, it needs very soft, acidic water and fine sand to sift.

region: Guiana Shield — Guyana, Suriname & northern Brazil
description: Closely related to S. jurupari, this eartheater is covered with pearly white spots on fins and flanks and has turquoise lines across the cheeks. It breeds more readily in aquaria than most of its genus, the pair carrying the larvae in their mouths.

region: Rio Negro & middle Amazon — Brazil & Colombia
description: Distinguished by a single large black spot high on the rear flank, this blackwater eartheater is golden with turquoise lines on the face. It sifts fine sand in soft, acidic water and broods its larvae in the mouth.

region: Paraguay & Guaporé basins — Brazil, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: A hardy Satanoperca of the Pantanal and Guaporé, brownish with a large dark mid-flank blotch and a spot at the tail base. It tolerates a wider range of water than Amazonian relatives and broods its larvae in the mouth.

A rheophilic cichlid of the Xingu's rapids that rests on the bottom propped on its broad pectoral fins, darting between stones against the current. Pairs dig a pit in gravel and cover their sticky eggs with sand grains and small pebbles.

A tiny pike cichlid from the rocky rapids of the Rio Tocantins, with a laterally compressed head and a dark band from snout to tail. It stalks small invertebrates among stones, and pairs spawn in narrow crevices.

A dwarf pike cichlid of clear Amazonian streams; males have rows of dark spots in the tail, while females show a pink-red belly and a white-ringed black spot in the dorsal fin. Pairs spawn in a cave and guard the fry for weeks.

Named 'eye on the back' for the white-ringed black ocellus in the female's dorsal fin, this dwarf pike cichlid lives among roots and leaf litter in blackwater. Females court males with their swollen, pink-purple bellies.

region: Coastal rivers of Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: A slender ambush predator of Guianan coastal rivers, dotted with pearly spots and marked with a light-ringed black spot behind the gill and an ocellus at the tail base. Pairs spawn in caves and defend their fry fiercely.

region: Paraguay & Guaporé basins — Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A medium-sized pike cichlid of the Pantanal and Paraná with a dark lateral band and a yellow-ringed black spot above the pectoral fin. It tolerates cooler water than Amazonian relatives and spawns in caves.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco — Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: One of the largest pike cichlids, a blackwater ambush piscivore peppered with small dark spots over a greenish-grey body. It needs a very large tank and is kept mainly by specialists and public aquaria.

region: Upper Orinoco & upper Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: The tallest angelfish, from soft, acidic blackwater tributaries such as the Atabapo and Inírida, distinguished by a notch above the snout and reddish-brown bars. Wild fish need very warm, soft water and shoal in groups among submerged branches.

region: Central Amazon basin, Brazil (Solimões–Amazonas & lower Rio Negro)
description: The smallest angelfish, with a straight profile in front of the dorsal fin (no nuchal notch) and a distinct dark blotch at the base of the dorsal fin. It is shyer and more delicate than the domesticated P. scalare.
A line-bred angelfish carrying a double dose of the black gene, so the whole body and fins are velvety black and the red iris stands out. Behaviour and breeding are those of the wild species.

A line-bred angelfish in which the vertical bars are replaced by irregular black-and-silver marbling that differs on every fish and often darkens with age. It has the same biology as the wild species.
A recessive gold variety with no bars at all: a pale golden body, an orange crown on the head and nearly clear fins. It shares the biology of the wild species.
Combines the gold and marble genes: a golden body with an orange crown, broken by scattered black marbling patches. Same biology as the wild species.

A gold-marble variety selected for an orange head and back on a pale body with irregular black patches, reminiscent of koi; the orange intensifies when the fish is excited. Same biology as the wild species.
A pure white, highly reflective variety with no bars or markings, the fins clear and the iris red. It is genetically a gold variety and has the biology of the wild species.
A dominant pattern variety with extra vertical bars — typically four or more across the body instead of the wild type's two. Its biology is that of the wild species.
A smokey-line variety in which the body is covered with dense dark spots on a brownish-grey ground, darkest on the upper body. It has the same biology as the wild species.

An albino variety lacking dark pigment: a creamy white body with faint ghost bars, a yellowish crown and a pink-red eye. Albinos are somewhat light-sensitive but otherwise share the wild species' biology.
A variety developed in the Philippines ('Pinoy' angels) carrying a gene that gives the body a powder-blue sheen, here with the standard silver bars. Same biology as the wild species.

region: Rio Negro basin & lower Amazon tributaries (e.g. Trombetas), Brazil
description: The Heckel discus of Rio Negro blackwater, recognised by its broad, dark central bar — the fifth of nine — far bolder than the others. It needs the softest, most acidic water of any discus and is more quarrelsome within groups.

region: Western Amazon — Solimões & tributaries (e.g. Lake Tefé), Brazil, Peru & Colombia
description: The western 'green' discus of the upper Amazon, whose best-known form from Lake Tefé carries red spots on the lower flanks and fins. Its blue-green lines are usually confined to the head, back and fins.
The blue discus of the central Amazon, brownish with wavy blue lines that in prized 'royal blue' fish cover the whole body. Its taxonomy is disputed and many authors include it in S. aequifasciatus.
A solid, unpatterned bright-blue strain developed by Asian breeders from turquoise lines, with no bars or lines left on the body. Like all domestic discus it needs very warm, clean, soft water.

A strain developed in Thailand in the early 1990s with orange-red markings over a pale cream body and the dark bars suppressed; scattered black 'pepper' spots are typical of the line. Same biology as other domestic discus.
One of the classic domestic strains, selectively bred from wild blue and green discus into bold turquoise stripes over a red-brown ground. Behaviour and care match other domestic discus.
A pigeon-blood-derived strain with an almost solid orange-red body, bars largely suppressed and dark-rimmed fins. Same biology as other domestic discus.

A strain with more than the usual nine bars and dense, very fine wavy lines that resemble snake scales; it arose in Southeast Asian breeding farms in the late 1990s. Same biology as other domestic discus.
A strain in which the turquoise lines break up into dense round red spots, giving a leopard-like body; it was developed from red-spotted green discus. Same biology as other domestic discus.
A strain with a bright red body and a contrasting yellow-white face, named after the colours of the cigarette packet. Same biology as other domestic discus.
A pigeon-blood-line strain in which the orange-red lines cross to form a grid of small squares over a pale ground. Same biology as other domestic discus.
A pigeon-blood-derived strain with a clear golden-yellow body and almost no pattern, the fins edged darker. Same biology as other domestic discus.
An all-white strain with no pattern at all, its red eye standing out against the pale body and fins. Same biology as other domestic discus.

A large, disc-like cichlid of flooded Amazonian forests that feeds heavily on plants, fruit and algae. Adults bear a big black wedge on the flank, and both parents feed their fry on skin mucus, as discus do.

The common severum of the Amazon, a deep-bodied greenish-gold cichlid whose dark bar between the rear dorsal and anal fins mimics an eyespot; adults lose most of the other bars. Males show red-brown vermiculations on the head, and pairs spawn on stone or wood and guard the fry together.

region: Orinoco & upper Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: The true Heros severus of the Orinoco and Rio Negro, which typically shows more distinct dark bars than the widespread H. efasciatus. It lives in soft, acidic blackwater among submerged wood and roots.
A spotted severum from the Rio Negro, yellowish with irregular dark blotches along the upper flank. Like its relatives it is a partly herbivorous substrate spawner of slow, wooded waters.
A xanthistic line-bred severum, usually sold under the name Heros severus, with a golden-yellow body and orange-red spots on the head of males. Its biology matches the wild species.

region: Amazon & Paraguay basins — Brazil, Bolivia, Peru & Paraguay
description: The festivum or flag cichlid, a peaceful, laterally compressed cichlid of quiet, vegetated floodplain waters, crossed by a black diagonal band from mouth to dorsal tip. Pairs spawn on leaves, often near the surface, and both parents guard the brood.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco — Brazil, Colombia & Venezuela
description: The Rio Negro and Orinoco counterpart of the festivum, with the same black band from mouth to dorsal tip and often a stronger blue-green sheen. It prefers soft, acidic blackwater among submerged branches and plants.

A robust cichlid of flooded Amazonian forest whose colours shift with mood from green to deep red-brown, always with a dark blotch mid-flank and green spangles on the head. Pairs are attentive parents, and it is relatively peaceful for its size.

A deep-bodied cichlid of blackwater floodplains, chocolate- to rust-brown with a dark blotch mid-flank and a steep forehead. It is shy and fairly peaceful for its size, and pairs spawn on submerged wood or stone.

region: Amazon basin — Peru, Colombia, Brazil & French Guiana
description: A large, intelligent cichlid of Amazonian floodplain lakes and slow rivers, named for the orange-ringed eyespot at the base of its tail. Oscars learn to recognise their keepers, rearrange their tanks, and pairs guard hundreds of fry.
The classic tiger oscar, a line-bred form with bold red-orange tiger stripes and blotches on a velvety black body. It has the size, intelligence and needs of the wild species.
A line-bred oscar in which the red pigment covers almost the whole flank, leaving a dark back and black fins. Same biology as the wild species.
An albino oscar lacking black pigment: white with red-orange tiger markings and pink-red eyes. It shares the wild species' size, behaviour and needs.

region: Paraguay basin & southern Amazon (Guaporé) — Brazil, Bolivia & Paraguay
description: A darker, less ornate relative of the common oscar; adults usually lack the row of ocelli along the dorsal-fin base but keep the ringed eyespot on the tail. It is seldom imported but shares the oscar's bold, intelligent behaviour.

region: Guiana Shield rivers — Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: A powerful predator of Guianan rivers with three gold-ringed dark blotches on the flank and an eyespot on the tail. Pairs guard their eggs and fry for weeks; it grows far too large for home tanks and is mainly seen in public aquaria.

The most widespread Amazonian peacock bass, yellow-green with three dark vertical blotches and a ringed eyespot on the tail. Breeding males develop a fatty nuchal hump, and both parents defend the fry.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco — Brazil, Venezuela & Colombia
description: The largest peacock bass: non-breeding 'paca' fish are grey-green with rows of pale spots, while breeding 'açu' fish turn golden with three bold dark bars and a nuchal hump. A blackwater top predator kept only in very large public aquaria.
The yellow peacock bass of the Tocantins–Araguaia, golden with three dark bars and white spots on the dorsal and tail fins. It has been widely introduced elsewhere in Brazil for sport fishing.

region: Orinoco & upper Rio Negro — Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: Named for the Orinoco, this peacock bass wears three large, round, gold-ringed black spots along the flank rather than bars. Pairs nest on firm substrate and guard their schooling fry.

The blue peacock bass of the Tocantins–Araguaia, distinguished by five dark vertical bars on a blue-grey to greenish body. Like other Cichla it is a voracious piscivore suited only to very large aquaria.

region: Amazon basin — Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador & Bolivia
description: A robust, widespread Amazonian acara, called the saddle cichlid for the dark blotch where its lateral band ends mid-flank. Pairs dig pits and guard their fry, and it tolerates a wide range of water.

The Meta acara of the Colombian llanos, bright yellow with metallic blue spangles on the face and a dark blotch mid-flank. A typical Aequidens, it forms pairs that spawn on flat stones and guard their brood.
A hardy acara from Trinidad and northern South America, bronze-green with dark bars and electric-blue lines across the face and scales. Pairs spawn on flat stones and are devoted parents.

A line-bred acara of intense metallic blue with orange edging on the dorsal fin; whether it is pure A. pulcher or of hybrid origin is still debated. It stays smaller and calmer than the wild blue acara.

region: Pacific slope rivers of Ecuador & northern Peru
description: The green terror of Pacific-slope rivers, studded with metallic green-blue scales; males of the 'gold saum' form edge their dorsal and tail fins in orange and grow a nuchal hump. It is a strong, aggressive cichlid that forms pairs to breed.

region: Pacific slope rivers of northern Peru
description: Described in 2009, this close relative of the green terror is sold as the 'silver saum', its dorsal and tail fins edged white rather than orange. It is slightly smaller but similarly aggressive.

region: Paraguay–Paraná & Guaporé basins — Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay & Argentina
description: A small, feisty acara with a dark band running obliquely from the eye toward the rear of the dorsal fin. Pairs spawn on a leaf or stone and then carry the larvae in their mouths.

region: Orinoco delta & Guianas — Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname & French Guiana
description: A shy, peaceful cichlid of slow, leaf-strewn coastal creeks, cream to tan with a dark keyhole-shaped spot on the upper flank and a dark bar through the eye. Pairs spawn on leaves or stones, and individuals can live for around a decade.

region: Amazon basin & Guianas — Brazil, Peru & Guyana
description: A sand-sifting cichlid of Amazonian and Guianan rivers whose males trail long, red-tipped filaments from the dorsal fin. Pairs excavate burrows beneath rocks or roots to spawn in, throwing up mounds of sand.

A stocky cichlid of Guianan coastal rivers, cream-yellow with a bold black bar mid-flank and another through the eye; males develop a nuchal hump and a red-edged dorsal fin. Pairs spawn in caves or under stones and guard their fry together.

A Guianacara of Surinamese and French Guianan rivers, silvery-yellow with a bold black bar below the dorsal fin and a dark stripe through the eye; males have a red-edged dorsal. Pairs breed in caves and are attentive parents.

An acara from clear Andean-foothill streams of the Río Aguaytía in Peru, greyish with dark bars and a dark band along the flank. Related to Bujurquina, it spawns on stone and the parents then brood the larvae in their mouths.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco — Brazil, Venezuela & Colombia
description: The original 'parrot cichlid', a large, deep-bodied blackwater species with a greenish body peppered with black spots and a rosy throat in adults. It is relatively peaceful for its size but needs a very large tank of soft, acidic water.

A subtropical cichlid of the Río de la Plata region whose dark bars and greenish sheen change rapidly with mood, hence 'chameleon cichlid'. Released aquarium fish have established populations in southern Portugal and Spain.

region: Pacific & Atlantic slopes of Guatemala, El Salvador & Honduras
description: A small, tough and famously prolific cichlid of Central American streams, blue-grey with eight or nine black bars; unusually, the female is the more colourful sex, with orange on her belly and fins. Pairs dig out a cave and fiercely defend clouds of fry.

A leucistic (not albino) line of the convict cichlid lacking black pigment, so the body is pinkish-white with dark eyes and females keep their orange belly patches. It is as hardy and prolific as the wild type.

Split from the convict cichlid in 2007, this close relative is sold as the 'Honduran Red Point'. Its bars are fainter than the convict's and its fins carry warmer tones, but it shares the same cave-spawning, fiercely protective breeding.

region: Atlantic slope of Honduras, Nicaragua & Costa Rica (incl. Lakes Nicaragua & Managua)
description: A deep-bodied cichlid of lakes and slow, weedy rivers whose long, high dorsal and anal fins give it a sunfish-like outline. Breeding pairs darken to near-black and guard their brood on open substrate.

region: Pacific & Atlantic slopes of Honduras, Nicaragua & Costa Rica
description: Unique among Neotropical cichlids in having tricuspid, algae-scraping teeth, this small species is golden-yellow with a dark lateral band. Breeding pairs flush black along the lower body and grow remarkably colourful, hence the name.

region: Yucatán Peninsula & Usumacinta basin — Mexico, Belize & Guatemala
description: A Yucatán cichlid of slow, clear rivers and lagoons that flares its gill covers to flash a fiery red throat and gold-ringed black spots at rivals, rather than fighting outright. Pairs dig pits in sand and guard their fry together.

region: Atlantic slope of Guatemala, Belize & Honduras
description: A Thorichthys of Caribbean-slope rivers, golden with turquoise spangles and, like the firemouth, a gold-ringed black spot on the gill cover that it flashes in display. Males trail elongated tips from the dorsal and anal fins.

A Mexican Thorichthys densely covered in turquoise spangles, with a reddish belly and a row of dark blotches along the mid-flank. Like its relatives it sifts sand for food and displays by flaring its spotted gill covers.

region: Atlantic slope of Guatemala, Belize & Honduras
description: A small Central American cichlid recognised by its turquoise-blue iris; males develop a nuchal hump and a yellowish body, while females stay darker-barred. Pairs spawn in caves and are fierce defenders for their size.

A small Costa Rican cichlid named for the dark T-shaped mark formed by a mid-flank bar joined to a short lateral band. It is relatively mild for a Central American, spawns in caves, and is placed in Amatitlania by some authors.

region: Río Grande (Bravo) & Gulf-slope rivers — northeastern Mexico & southern Texas, USA
description: The only cichlid native to the United States, grey-green and densely spangled with pearly blue spots. Breeding fish turn black on the lower body and pale above, and males develop a nuchal hump.

region: Río Pánuco basin & Gulf slope of Tamaulipas–Veracruz, Mexico
description: Often sold as the 'green Texas' cichlid, this Gulf-slope Mexican species carries larger, brighter turquoise spangles than H. cyanoguttatus. Like other Herichthys, breeding adults turn black below and pale above.

Endemic to the desert spring pools of Cuatro Ciénegas, this endangered cichlid is famous for jaw polymorphism: individuals develop either slender teeth for soft food or massive molar-like teeth for crushing snails. It is kept mainly in conservation programmes and public aquaria.

region: Usumacinta basin & Yucatán — Mexico, Guatemala & Belize
description: Long sold as Vieja synspilus, the redhead cichlid has a crimson-to-purple head and a black blotch running back into the tail — 'melanurus' means black-tailed. It is a largely herbivorous, pair-bonding cichlid of lakes and slow rivers.

region: Atlantic slope from southern Mexico to Panama
description: A large Caribbean-slope cichlid named for the black spot on its tail base and better known for the broad black 'belt' across its mid-flank; adults have a red throat and red-edged fins. It enters brackish coastal lagoons and feeds mainly on plants and detritus.
A Usumacinta cichlid with two dark longitudinal bands along the flank, a purplish-red head and blue-spotted scales in adults. Like other Vieja it feeds largely on plant matter and detritus.

region: Papaloapan & Coatzacoalcos basins incl. Lake Catemaco, Mexico
description: A Gulf-slope Mexican cichlid whose dark vertical bars, crossed by a lateral band, leave pale 'windows' along the flank, hence fenestrata. It is a robust, largely herbivorous species of rivers and Lake Catemaco.

region: Lakes Nicaragua & Managua and the San Juan basin — Nicaragua & Costa Rica
description: Named for the gold colour morph that a minority of wild fish develop as they mature, the Midas cichlid is otherwise grey with dark bars; breeding males grow a large nuchal hump. Pairs defend territories around rocky caves in the great Nicaraguan lakes.

A Nicaraguan lake cichlid named for its thick, fleshy lips, used to pry invertebrates from rock crevices. Aquarium 'red devils' are mostly orange-red and often hybridised with the Midas cichlid; wild fish may be grey-barred or gold.

Endemic to the deep crater lake Apoyo, this slender, high-finned cichlid evolved from Midas-like ancestors within the lake as an open-water forager, a classic case of sympatric speciation. It is greyish with dark bars, though gold individuals occur.

region: Pacific slope from southern Mexico to El Salvador
description: The trimac of Pacific-slope rivers, named for its three black blotches — behind the head, mid-flank and at the tail base — on a greenish-gold body with an orange-red throat. Males grow a nuchal hump, and it is notably aggressive.

region: Atlantic slope of Honduras, Nicaragua & Costa Rica (incl. Lakes Nicaragua & Managua)
description: The jaguar cichlid of Nicaraguan lakes and lowland rivers, silvery with a purplish sheen and a dense pattern of black spots and blotches. A powerful ambush predator with a highly protrusible jaw, it needs a very large tank.

region: Atlantic & Pacific slopes of Honduras, Nicaragua & Costa Rica
description: One of the largest Central American cichlids, a formidable predator with big canine-like teeth; adult males turn golden-yellow with black spots, while females keep a broad dark lateral band. It is among the most aggressive cichlids kept.

region: Motagua & Pacific-slope basins of Guatemala & Honduras
description: A medium-sized Parachromis from Guatemala and Honduras, reddish-brown with a band of dark blotches along the flank and fine red speckling. Like its larger relatives it is a predatory and very protective parent.

region: Atlantic slope from southern Mexico to Costa Rica
description: The yellowjacket cichlid, yellow with a row of dark blotches along the mid-flank and black spotting on the head and fins. A medium-sized predator of slow, vegetated waters along the Caribbean slope.

region: Atlantic slope of Nicaragua & Costa Rica (incl. Lake Nicaragua)
description: A Nicaraguan cichlid with a down-turned mouth and a golden body shading to blue-green on the head, marked by a black spot mid-flank. Unusually, it lays non-adhesive eggs in a dug pit or cave rather than sticking them to a surface.

region: Atlantic slope from southern Mexico to Honduras
description: Named after the 1920s boxer for its pugnacious temperament, the Jack Dempsey is dark purplish-grey covered in iridescent blue-green and gold spangles, with a red-edged dorsal fin. Pairs are devoted parents that dig pits and defend their fry vigorously.

A line-bred Jack Dempsey in which iridescent spangling covers almost the entire body, making it shimmer electric blue. It stays smaller, is less robust and is usually milder in temperament than the wild form.

region: Lakes Nicaragua & Managua and rivers of Costa Rica
description: A small, feisty rock-dweller that scrapes algae and tiny invertebrates from stones; normally pale grey with one dark mid-flank bar, it inverts to a black body with a pale bar when breeding. Its rock-grazing life earned it the name 'poor man's Tropheus'.

region: Atlantic slope from southern Mexico (Yucatán) to Nicaragua; introduced in Florida
description: A hardy cichlid of Yucatán lagoons, cenotes and mangroves that tolerates everything from fresh to sea-strength water, marked by dark bars and a turquoise-ringed eyespot at the tail base. It is an established invasive species in southern Florida.

region: Atlantic slope of southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize & Honduras
description: Also called the tricolor cichlid, it is bright yellow with a black lateral band, a red belly and turquoise spangles on the head and fins. A small but aggressive predator of flowing rivers, its pairs are fierce guardians of their fry.

region: Atrato, Magdalena & Tuira basins — Colombia & eastern Panama
description: One of the largest cichlids in the world, the umbee is a massive, dark green predator covered in turquoise and gold spangles. It is kept only by specialists with very large aquaria and in public aquaria.

A large, herbivorous cichlid whose chisel-like front teeth — the source of the genus name — crop leaves and fallen fruit in the Usumacinta and Grijalva rivers. It is olive-yellow with a row of dark blotches along the flank.

region: Usumacinta & Grijalva basins and Yucatán — Mexico, Guatemala & Belize
description: A large, lurking predator whose jaws shoot forward in a long tube to engulf prey. Wild fish are bronze-olive with a row of dark blotches, while a red-orange morph is also bred for the trade.

scientificName: hybrid (Amphilophus × Vieja and other Central American cichlids)
description: A man-made hybrid of several Central American cichlids, prized for its huge nuchal hump ('kok'), pearly spangles and a row of black 'flower' blotches along the flank. Unlike the blood parrot it is fertile, and its aggression means it is usually kept alone.

A man-made hybrid with a rounded body, a small, beak-like vertical mouth that cannot fully close, and solid orange-red colour. Males are usually sterile, though pairs still clean a site, spawn and guard their infertile eggs.
